Claude Sabbah C. SabbahCMLS, CNRS, École polytechnique, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, 91128 Palaiseau cedex, France Email address: Claude.Sabbah@polytechnique.edu URL: https://perso.pages.math.cnrs.fr/users/claude.sabbah and Jeng-Daw Yu J.-D. Abstract.

We consider the complex analogues of symmetric power moments of cubic exponential sums. These are symmetric powers of the classical Airy differential equation. We show that their de Rham cohomologies underlie an arithmetic Hodge structure in the sense of Anderson and we compute their Hodge numbers by means of the irregular Hodge filtration, which is indexed by rational numbers, on their realizations as exponential mixed Hodge structures. The main result is that all Hodge numbers are either zero or one.

Key words and phrases: 
Airy differential equation, mixed Hodge structure, exponential mixed Hodge structure, irregular Hodge filtration
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
14C30, 14D07, 32G20, 32S40, 34M35

1. Introduction

Families of cubic exponential sums attached to the polynomial x3+z​xx^{3}+zx in xx over finite fields and their symmetric power moments over zz (Airy moments) have been considered in analogy with moments of Kloosterman sums for example, and much is already known about the corresponding LL functions (see [11, 12] and the references therein). For the analogous moments of Kloosterman sums, a conjecture of Broadhurst and Roberts, concerning the precise functional equations satisfied by the corresponding global LL functions, has been proved in [7] (except the exact local information at prime 22 when kk is even). In such a case, a pure Nori motive Mk\Motive_{k} defined over 𝐐\mathbf{Q} is attached to the kk-moments. One of the main arguments is to prove that the associated Galois representation of Mk\Motive_{k} is potentially automorphic, which relies on a theorem of Patrikis and Taylor [19], owing to the property proved in [7], that all nonzero Hodge numbers of Mk\Motive_{k} are equal to one.

For Airy moments, a strictly similar strategy to understand the Galois theoretic properties of the corresponding motivic object Mk\Motive_{k} is not possible, basically because Mk\Motive_{k} is not a Nori motive, but an ulterior motive in the sense of Anderson [3]. Nevertheless, Hodge theory can be developed in this context (arithmetic Hodge structure in the sense of Anderson), with the caveat that the Hodge numbers h𝗉,𝗊h^{\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q}} may occur for rational exponents 𝗉,𝗊\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q} subject to 𝗉+𝗊∈𝐙\mathsf{p}+\mathsf{q}\in\mathbf{Z}.

A similar notion of Hodge structure, that we call a finite monodromic mixed Hodge structure as defined in Section 2, has been considered by Scherk and Steenbrink [34] when analyzing the join of two mixed Hodge structures equipped with an automorphism of finite order. Already in [36], Steenbrink attached to the mixed Hodge structure on the nearby cycles and vanishing cycles of a holomorphic function with an isolated singularity, a Hodge polynomial in 𝐙[t1/m,t−1/m]\mathbf{Z}[t^{1/m},t^{-1/m}], where mm is the order of the semi-simple part of the monodromy. He conjectured a behaviour of the Hodge polynomial under Thom-Sebastiani sums as modeled in [34], a conjecture which was proved by M. Saito [32] and later received a proof using motivic integration in [10].

The complex analogue of the Airy kk-moment is the kk-th symmetric product Symk⁡Ai\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai} of the Airy differential equation Ai\mathrm{Ai} on the affine line 𝔸z1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{z}, defined by the classical Airy operator ∂z2−z\partial_{z}^{2}-z. We regard Ai\mathrm{Ai} as a rank-two vector bundle on 𝔸z1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{z} with a connection having ∞\infty as its only singularity, which is irregular of slope 3/23/2 and has irregularity number equal to 33. Therefore, Symk⁡Ai\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai} is regarded as a rank (k+1)(k+1) vector bundle with connection on 𝔸z1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{z} having a singularity at infinity only. Contrary to the case of the Kloosterman connection, the de Rham cohomology HdR1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}) does not naturally underlie a mixed Hodge structure (again reflecting the fact that Mk\Motive_{k} is not classical). However, it is the de Rham fiber of an exponential mixed Hodge structure with finite monodromy, hence underlies a finite monodromic mixed Hodge structure (see Section 5.c). As indicated above, such structures provide an alternative approach to the arithmetic Hodge structures of Anderson, and they are more closely related to exponential mixed Hodge structures defined by Kontsevich and Soibelman [15]. As in [7], we recover the 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-indexed Hodge filtration of this finite monodromic mixed Hodge structure as the irregular Hodge filtration on the de Rham fiber HdR1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}). The main result of this article is the computation of the corresponding irregular Hodge numbers, opening the way to applying the results of Patrikis and Taylor on the arithmetic of the underlying ulterior motive Mk\Motive_{k}.

Theorem 1.1.

Let kk be an integer ⩾2\geqslant 2 and set k′=⌊(k−1)/2⌋k^{\prime}=\left\lfloor(k-1)/2\right\rfloor. Then the de Rham cohomology HdR1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}) naturally underlies a finite monodromic mixed Hodge structure and the Hodge numbers h𝗉𝗊=dimgrF𝗉​gr𝗉+𝗊W​HdR1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai)h^{\mathsf{p}\mathsf{q}}=\dim\gr_{F}^{\mathsf{p}}\gr^{W}_{\mathsf{p}+\mathsf{q}}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}) are all equal to one for the following (𝗉,𝗊)(\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q}) and vanish otherwise:

  • ∙\scriptscriptstyle\bullet

    kk odd, 𝗉+𝗊=k+1\mathsf{p}+\mathsf{q}=k+1 and 𝗉=13​(k+2​i)\mathsf{p}=\frac{1}{3}(k+2i), 1⩽i⩽k′+11\leqslant i\leqslant k^{\prime}+1,

  • ∙\scriptscriptstyle\bullet

    4|(k+2)4\mid(k+2), 𝗉+𝗊=k+1\mathsf{p}+\mathsf{q}=k+1 and min⁡{𝗉,𝗊}=13​(k+2​i)\min\{\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q}\}=\frac{1}{3}(k+2i), 1⩽i⩽k′/21\leqslant i\leqslant{k^{\prime}}/{2},

  • ∙\scriptscriptstyle\bullet

    4|k4\mid k and either 𝗉+𝗊=k+1\mathsf{p}+\mathsf{q}=k+1 with min⁡{𝗉,𝗊}=13​(k+2​i)\min\{\mathsf{p},\mathsf{q}\}=\frac{1}{3}(k+2i), 1⩽i⩽(k′−1)/21\leqslant i\leqslant{(k^{\prime}-1)}/{2}, or 𝗉=𝗊=(k+2)/2\mathsf{p}=\mathsf{q}={(k+2)}/{2}.

We are mostly interested in the middle de Rham cohomology, which is by definition the image im[HdR,c1(𝔸1,SymkAi)→HdR1(𝔸1,SymkAi)]\image[\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai})]. We show (Corollaries 5.14 and 5.22) that, with respect to the finite monodromic mixed Hodge structure on HdR1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}), it is equal to the weight (k+1)(k+1) subspace:

HdR,mid1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai)=Wk+1​HdR1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai).\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai})=W_{k+1}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}).

As a consequence of Theorem 1.1, the middle de Rham cohomology underlies a finite monodromic pure Hodge structure, and the corresponding Hodge numbers coincide with those of HdR1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}) if 4∤k4\nmid k, and are obtained by omitting the case 𝗉=𝗊=(k+2)/2\mathsf{p}=\mathsf{q}={(k+2)}/{2} if 4|k4\mid k.

Organization of the paper

The approach of the present article is much inspired from that of [7] on moments of Kloosterman connections. Sections 2–5 consist of a review of known properties of various tools that we use, together with complementary results in presence of an action of the group μ^=lim←m⁡𝐙/m​𝐙{\widehat{\mu}}=\varprojlim_{m}\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z}. In Section 5, we emphasize the decomposition of a finite monodromic exponential mixed Hodge structure (that we call a μ^{\widehat{\mu}}-exponential mixed Hodge structure for short) into its classical and non-classical parts. While the former can be treated with the same methods as in [7], the latter shows new Hodge-theoretic phenomena.

The main example of such an object is that attached to a regular function on 𝔸s1×V\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{s}\times V of the form sm​gs^{m}g (m⩾2m\geqslant 2), where g:V→𝔸1g:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1} is a regular function on a smooth quasi-projective variety. The corresponding non-classical μ^{\widehat{\mu}}-exponential mixed Hodge structure (Proposition 5.10) can be expressed by means of the mixed Hodge structure of the covering of V∖g−1​(0)V\smallsetminus g^{-1}(0) which is cyclic of degree mm and ramified along g−1​(0)g^{-1}(0). While this expression makes clear the ulterior motivic origin of this finite monodromic mixed Hodge structure, it does not help for computing Hodge numbers in Theorem 1.1. In order to handle the case of even kk in the theorem, we provide in Section 5.f an expression in terms of additive convolution with Kummer sheaves, which reduces the computation to a local (monodromic) computation similar to that used for the classical component modeled on that of [7].

In Section 6 we provide Hodge-theoretic properties for the moments of the generalized Airy equation of order n⩾2n\geqslant 2 (the case n=2n=2 being our main concern), yielding the finite monodromic mixed Hodge structure on the de Rham cohomologies of their symmetric powers Symk⁡Ain\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}_{n}, and an estimation of their weights. This is a variant of the techniques used in [7].

Once all these preliminaries are settled, the proof of Theorem 1.1 is achieved in Section 7. As in loc. cit., we play with two expressions of the de Rham cohomology, one computed in dimension one like H1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai)\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}) and the other one using the geometry of the function s3​∑i=1k(13​xi3−xi)s^{3}\sum_{i=1}^{k}(\frac{1}{3}x_{i}^{3}-x_{i}). The former provides in a simple way a basis of the de Rham cohomology and an associated filtration which satisfies the conclusion of the theorem, and the latter relates the computation of Hodge numbers to that of the corresponding irregular Hodge filtration on a suitable blow-up of ℙk+1\mathbb{P}^{k+1}. While the geometry is simple enough to enable us to conclude the proof if kk is odd by showing that the basis filtration is contained in the irregular Hodge filtration, we need supplementary arguments to conclude in the case of even kk, which occupies Sections 7.d–7.g. Although the idea is similar to that of [7], we need here to make use of a Hodge-theoretic inverse stationary phase formula, as we already did in [29], to recover enough information on the Hodge filtration.

2. Finite monodromic mixed Hodge structures

We review and adapt results of [34, p. 661]. Let μ^=lim←m⁡𝐙/m​𝐙{\widehat{\mu}}=\varprojlim_{m}\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z} be the profinite completion of the abelian group 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. Let 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(𝐐)\Vect(\mathbf{Q}) be the category of finite-dimensional 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-vector spaces and let 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍μ^⁡(𝐐)\Vect^{\widehat{\mu}}(\mathbf{Q}) denote the category consisting of a finite-dimensional 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-vector space H𝐐H_{\mathbf{Q}} together with an action of μ^{\widehat{\mu}} through a finite quotient 𝐙/m​𝐙\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z} for some mm. Equivalently, by setting TT to be the action of the topological generator 1∈μ^1\in{\widehat{\mu}}, an object of 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍μ^⁡(𝐐)\Vect^{\widehat{\mu}}(\mathbf{Q}) is a pair (H𝐐,T)(H_{\mathbf{Q}},T) consisting of the space H𝐐H_{\mathbf{Q}} together with an automorphism TT of finite order. Each group ring 𝐐⁡[𝐙/m​𝐙]\mathbf{Q}[\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z}] has the orthogonal decomposition

𝐐⁡[𝐙/m​𝐙]=e1​𝐐​[𝐙/m​𝐙]⊕e≠1​𝐐​[𝐙/m​𝐙]\mathbf{Q}[\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z}]=e_{1}\mathbf{Q}[\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z}]\oplus e_{\neq 1}\mathbf{Q}[\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z}]

where e1=1m​∑g∈𝐙/m​𝐙ge_{1}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{g\in\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z}}g is the projector into the invariant part and e≠1=1−e1e_{\neq 1}=1-e_{1}, and the decomposition is compatible with the quotient 𝐙/m′​𝐙→𝐙/m​𝐙\mathbf{Z}/m^{\prime}\mathbf{Z}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z} for m|m′m\mid m^{\prime}. Correspondingly for a given object (H𝐐,T)(H_{\mathbf{Q}},T) of 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍μ^⁡(𝐐)\Vect^{\widehat{\mu}}(\mathbf{Q}), there is a canonical decomposition in 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍μ^⁡(𝐐)\Vect^{\widehat{\mu}}(\mathbf{Q})

where TT has no non-trivial invariant in H𝐐,≠1H_{\mathbf{Q},\neq 1}. Let μm⊂𝐂×\mu_{m}\subset\mathbf{C}^{\times} be the cyclic subgroup of order mm and μm∗=μm∖{1}\mu_{m}^{*}=\mu_{m}\smallsetminus\{1\}. In terms of the eigenvalue decomposition H𝐂=⨁ζ∈μmHζH_{\mathbf{C}}=\mathop{\textstyle\bigoplus}\displaylimits_{\zeta\in\mu_{m}}H_{\zeta} where H𝐂=H𝐐⊗𝐂H_{\mathbf{C}}=H_{\mathbf{Q}}\otimes\mathbf{C} and T=ζ​IdT=\zeta\id on HζH_{\zeta}, one has H𝐐,1⊗𝐂=H1H_{\mathbf{Q},1}\otimes\mathbf{C}=H_{1} and H𝐐,≠1⊗𝐂=⨁ζ∈μm∗HζH_{\mathbf{Q},\neq 1}\otimes\mathbf{C}=\mathop{\textstyle\bigoplus}\displaylimits_{\zeta\in\mu_{m}^{*}}H_{\zeta}. Remark 2.6.

  1. (1)

    (The spectrum) If TT has order mm, the Hodge polynomial

    ∑𝗉∈1m​𝐙(dimgrFμ^𝗉​H𝐂)⋅t𝗉\sum_{\mathsf{p}\in\frac{1}{m}\mathbf{Z}}(\dim\gr^{\mathsf{p}}_{F_{\widehat{\mu}}}H_{\mathbf{C}})\cdot t^{\mathsf{p}}

    was considered by Steenbrink [36] for the vanishing cycles of an isolated singularity of a holomorphic function and, in the case of a quasi-homogeneous isolated singularity, was compared to the Poincaré polynomial attached to the Newton filtration of the Jacobian quotient of the singularity.

  2. (2)

    (Relation with Anderson’s arithmetic Hodge structures) Anderson has defined in [3, §6.1] the notion of arithmetic Hodge structure. We will omit his condition (6.1.5) for the moment, which is related to the rational structure of the de Rham component of the arithmetic Hodge structure. Any such structure is the direct sum of pure structures of some integral weight. Then the notion of pure arithmetic Hodge structure (without Condition (6.1.5) of loc. cit.) is related to that of a μ^{\widehat{\mu}}-pure Hodge structure. Indeed, assume that a finite-dimensional 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-vector space H𝐐H_{\mathbf{Q}} with the decomposition

    is a pure arithmetic Hodge structure of weight w∈𝐙w\in\mathbf{Z}. 3. Perverse sheaves on the affine line

Notation 3.1.

We will often use the following diagram involving the affine line (whose coordinate may take various names):

{0}⸦i→𝔸1j←⸧𝔾m.\{0\}\mathrel{\lhook\joinrel\mathchoice{\xrightarrow{\textstyle\kern 4.0pti\kern 3.0pt}}{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\longrightarrow}}}{}{}}\mathbb{A}^{\!1}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\xleftarrow{\textstyle~j~}}{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle j}}{{\longleftarrow}}}{}{}\joinrel\rhook}\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}.

3.a. 𝒌{\boldsymbol{k}}-Perverse sheaves

We equip the affine line 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{\!1} (coordinate θ\theta) with its analytic structure, which we denote by 𝔸1​a​n\mathbb{A}^{\!1\mathrm{an}}. However, for the sake of simplicity, we simply denote it by 𝔸θ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta} or 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{\!1} in this section.

We refer to [14, Chap. 2] for details on the next results. Let 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(𝐤)\Vect({\boldsymbol{k}}) be the category of 𝒌{\boldsymbol{k}}-vector spaces for some fixed field 𝒌{\boldsymbol{k}}, and let 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏⁡(𝐤)\Perv({\boldsymbol{k}}) be the category of perverse sheaves on 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{\!1} of 𝒌{\boldsymbol{k}}-vector spaces. The field 𝒌{\boldsymbol{k}} being fixed, we simply write 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍,𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏\Vect,\Perv. The additive convolution product ⋆\star on 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏\Perv does not take values in 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏\Perv. However, let 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0\Perv_{0} be the full subcategory of 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏\Perv whose objects consist of perverse sheaves with zero global cohomology. It is equipped with a tensor structure given by ⋆\star and there is a natural projector Π:𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏→𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0\Pi:\Perv\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\Perv_{0} given by the additive convolution with j!𝒌𝔾mj_{!}{\boldsymbol{k}}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}. There is a functorial morphism ℱ→Π⁡(ℱ)\mathcal{F}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\Pi(\mathcal{F}) in 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏\Perv whose kernel and cokernel are constant perverse sheaves. For a perverse sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} on 𝔸θ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta}, we denote by p​ψθ​ℱ\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\psi}_{\theta}\mathcal{F}, resp. p​ϕθ​ℱ\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\phi}_{\theta}\mathcal{F}, the space of nearby, resp. vanishing, cycles at θ=0\theta=0, equipped with its monodromy operator. The functor p​ϕθ\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\phi}_{\theta} decomposes with respect to eigenvalues of the semi-simple part of the monodromy as p​ϕθ,1⊕p​ϕθ,≠1\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\phi}_{\theta,1}\oplus\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\phi}_{\theta,\neq 1} where the second subscripts indicate the range of the eigenvalues. The two components behave differently when extended to mixed Hodge modules, and we have p​ϕθ,≠1=p​ψθ,≠1\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\phi}_{\theta,\neq 1}=\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\psi}_{\theta,\neq 1}.

The topological Fourier (or Laplace) transformations FT±\FT_{\pm}, for which we refer to [17, §VI.2] and [25, §1.b], transform objects of 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0\Perv_{0} to perverse sheaves on another copy of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}, with coordinate τ\tau, say, of the form 𝑹​j∗​ℒ​[1]\boldsymbol{R}j_{*}\mathcal{L}[1] for some local system ℒ\mathcal{L} on 𝔾mτ\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}{}_{\tau}. However, the datum of the perverse sheaf 𝑹​j∗​ℒ±​[1]=FT±⁡(ℱ)\boldsymbol{R}j_{*}\mathcal{L}_{\pm}[1]=\FT_{\pm}(\mathcal{F}) is in general not enough to recover ℱ\mathcal{F}, as Stokes data for 𝑹​j∗​ℒ±​[1]\boldsymbol{R}j_{*}\mathcal{L}_{\pm}[1] at infinity on 𝔸τ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau} are missing in this description. The case of monodromic perverse sheaves is simpler, as shown by Lemma 3.2 below, where FT\FT is either the ++ or the −- Fourier transformation, and FT−1\FT^{-1} is respectively the −- or the ++ Fourier transformation. For ℱ1,ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2} in 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0\Perv_{0}, we have j−1​FT⁡(ℱ1⋆ℱ2)​[−1]≃ℒ1⊗ℒ2j^{-1}\FT(\mathcal{F}_{1}\star\mathcal{F}_{2})[-1]\simeq\mathcal{L}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{L}_{2}. Taking the fiber at 11 of (FT⁡ℱ)​[−1](\FT\mathcal{F})[-1] is a fiber functor for the Tannakian category 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0\Perv_{0}.

Let 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0μ^\Perv_{0}^{\widehat{\mu}} denote the full tensor subcategory of 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0mon\Perv_{0}^{\mathrm{mon}} consisting of objects ℱ\mathcal{F} for which there exists a cyclic covering [m]:𝔸θm1→𝔸θ1[m]:\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta_{m}}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta} of degree m⩾1m\geqslant 1, written in coordinates as θm↦θ=(θm)m\theta_{m}\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\theta=(\theta_{m})^{m}, such that the pullback [m]−1​ℱ[m]^{-1}\mathcal{F} is an object of 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0cst\Perv_{0}^{\mathrm{cst}}. Proof.

We give details on this proof, as a similar argument will be used for exponential mixed Hodge structures (see Proposition 5.2). By the equivalence of Lemma 3.2(1), we can replace 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0μ^\Perv_{0}^{\widehat{\mu}} with the category of local systems ℒ\mathcal{L} on 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} with finite monodromy, and by Remark 3.4, the functor to 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍μ^\Vect^{\widehat{\mu}} is given, on a local system ℒ\mathcal{L} such that [m]−1​ℒ[m]^{-1}\mathcal{L} is constant, by ℒ↦(Γ⁡(𝔾m,[m]−1​ℒ),G)\mathcal{L}\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}(\Gamma(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},[m]^{-1}\mathcal{L}),G), where the action of G=𝐙/m​𝐙G=\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z} is that of the Galois group of the covering [m]:𝔾m→𝔾m[m]:\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}.

Conversely, given (V,G)(V,G) in 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍μ^\Vect^{\widehat{\mu}} where G=𝐙/m​𝐙G=\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z}, we define a local system ℒ\mathcal{L} with finite monodromy as follows. Let (𝒱,G)(\mathcal{V},G) be the constant local system on 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} with stalk VV and the induced GG-action. The local system [m]∗​𝒱[m]_{*}\mathcal{V} is equipped with the induced GG-action and the Galois GG-action. One checks that both functors are quasi-inverse to each other by using the property that, given (V,G)(V,G) as above, and equipping 𝒌m{\boldsymbol{k}}^{m} with the action of GG induced by the cyclic permutation of the standard basis vectors, then if one equips V⊗𝒌mV\otimes{\boldsymbol{k}}^{m} with its natural G×GG\times G-action, (V,G)(V,G) is isomorphic to (V⊗𝒌m)inv(V\otimes{\boldsymbol{k}}^{m})^{\mathrm{inv}} equipped with the induced GG-action, where inv{\mathrm{inv}} means invariants under the {(g−1,g)∣g∈G}\{(g^{-1},g)\mid g\in G\}-action.

One can then express a quasi-inverse functor of the functor p​ϕθ\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\phi}_{\theta} of the lemma as follows. Given (V,G)(V,G) in 𝖵𝖾𝖼𝗍μ^\Vect^{\widehat{\mu}}, one first associates with it the object of 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0cst\Perv_{0}^{\mathrm{cst}} with GG-action defined by (Π(i!V),G)(\Pi(i_{!}V),G), and then the object ℱ\mathcal{F} of 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0μ^\Perv_{0}^{\widehat{\mu}} defined as ([m]∗Π(i!V))inv([m]_{*}\Pi(i_{!}V))^{\mathrm{inv}}, with the same meaning as above for inv{\mathrm{inv}}. ∎

Remark 3.7.

Let [m]:𝔸θm1→𝔸1[m]:\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta_{m}}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1} be as above. If ℱ=j!ℒ[1]\mathcal{F}=j_{!}\mathcal{L}[1] belongs to 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0mon⁡(𝔸1)\Perv_{0}^{\mathrm{mon}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}), then

The drawback with the functor ℱ↦p​ϕθm,1​([m]−1​ℱ)\mathcal{F}\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\phi}_{\theta_{m},1}([m]^{-1}\mathcal{F}) is that it is a priori not compatible with the tensor structures. 4. Exponential mixed Hodge structures

In this section, we recall the construction due to Kontsevich and Soibelman [15, §4] of the exponential mixed Hodge structures Hc∙​(U,f)\mathrm{H}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}_{\mathrm{c}}(U,f) and H∙​(U,f)\mathrm{H}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}(U,f) attached to a regular function f:U→𝔸1f:U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1} on a smooth quasi-projective variety UU. We emphasize the weight properties in Proposition 4.7, together with the pure part Hmid∙​(U,f)\mathrm{H}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}_{\mathrm{mid}}(U,f).

4.a. A review of exponential mixed Hodge structures

By the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence, the definitions of 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0\Perv_{0} and of the functor Π\Pi can be translated to regular holonomic D𝔸1{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}}-modules, and, according to [15, §4] both can be lifted in a compatible way to the category 𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸θ1)\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta}) of mixed Hodge modules on 𝔸θ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta}. This gives rise to the category 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS of exponential mixed Hodge structures, which is a full subcategory of 𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸θ1)\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta}), and there is a projector Π:𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸θ1)→𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\Pi:\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\EMHS, which is an exact functor, together with a functorial morphism NH→Π⁡(NH)N^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\Pi(N^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}) in 𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸θ1)\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta}) whose kernel and cokernel are constant mixed Hodge modules. Each object of 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS has a perverse realization in 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0\Perv_{0} and the projector Π:𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸θ1)→𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\Pi:\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\EMHS realizes as Π:𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏→𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0\Pi:\Perv\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\Perv_{0} of Section 3. Each object of 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS is equipped with a weight filtration in 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS, defined from that in 𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸θ1)\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta}) by the formula

WℓEMHS​Π​(N)=Π⁡(Wℓ​N)W^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{EMHS}}_{\ell}\Pi(N)=\Pi(W_{\ell}N)

4.b. Weight and irregular Hodge filtrations on the de Rham fiber

We recall here the general framework, for which we refer e.g. to [29, Chap. 3]. We denote by θ^\widehat{\theta} the variable which is Fourier dual to θ\theta. Let NHN^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} be a mixed Hodge module on 𝔸θ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta}, with (N,F∙​N,W∙​N)(N,F^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}N,W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}N) as the underlying bifiltered 𝐂[θ]⟨∂θ⟩\mathbf{C}[\theta]\langle\partial_{\theta}\rangle-module and (ℱ,W∙​ℱ)(\mathcal{F},W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}\mathcal{F}) as the underlying filtered 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-perverse sheaf.

Weight filtration

Fourier transformation sends these data to a filtered 𝐂[θ^]⟨∂θ^⟩\mathbf{C}[\widehat{\theta}]\langle\partial_{\widehat{\theta}}\rangle-module (FTθ⁡N,W∙​FTθ​N)(\FT_{\theta}N,W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}\FT_{\theta}N), with W∙​FTθ​N:=FT⁡W∙​NW_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}\FT_{\theta}N:=\FT W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}N, corresponding, via the de Rham functor, to the filtered perverse sheaf (FTθ⁡ℱ,W∙​FT⁡ℱ)(\FT_{\theta}\mathcal{F},W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}\FT\mathcal{F}) on 𝔸θ^1​a​n\mathbb{A}^{\!1\mathrm{an}}_{\widehat{\theta}} already considered in Section 3. Restricting FTθ⁡N\FT_{\theta}N, resp. FTθ⁡ℱ\FT_{\theta}\mathcal{F}, to θ^=1\widehat{\theta}=1 yields the de Rham fiber HdR1​(𝔸θ1,N⊗Eθ)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},N\otimes E^{\theta}), resp. the Betti fiber (FTθ⁡ℱ)1(\FT_{\theta}\mathcal{F})_{1}, which is a finite-dimensional vector space over 𝐂\mathbf{C} resp. 𝐐\mathbf{Q}. Moreover, additive convolution ⋆\star on 𝐂[θ]⟨∂θ⟩\mathbf{C}[\theta]\langle\partial_{\theta}\rangle-modules induces tensor product of de Rham fibers. By exactness of the de Rham fiber functor, which follows from exactness of FTθ\FT_{\theta} and the 𝐂⁡[θ^,θ^−1]\mathbf{C}[\widehat{\theta},\widehat{\theta}^{-1}]-freeness of j+​FTθ​Nj^{+}\FT_{\theta}N, the natural morphism

is injective and its image is a filtration W∙​HdR1​(𝔸θ1,N⊗Eθ)W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},N\otimes E^{\theta}). Moreover, W∙​NHW_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}N^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} and W∙EMHS​NHW^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{EMHS}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}N^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} have the same de Rham resp. Betti image (same argument as for p​ϕθ\raisebox{4.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\phi}_{\theta} in Remark 4.1). We thus have a tensor product behavior of the WW-filtration analogous to that occurring in Definition 2.7:

W∙​HdR1​(𝔸θ1,(N′⋆N′′)⊗Eθ)≃W∙​HdR1​(𝔸θ1,N′⊗Eθ)⊗W∙​HdR1​(𝔸θ1,N′′⊗Eθ).W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},(N^{\prime}\star N^{\prime\prime})\otimes E^{\theta})\simeq W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},N^{\prime}\otimes E^{\theta})\otimes W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},N^{\prime\prime}\otimes E^{\theta}).

Irregular Hodge filtration

On the other hand, the Hodge filtration F∙​NF^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}N gives rise to the Deligne filtration FDel∙​(N⊗Eθ)F_{\mathrm{Del}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}(N\otimes E^{\theta}) (see [26, §6]), which is indexed by 𝐙−A\mathbf{Z}-A for some finite subset A⊂[0,1)∩𝐐A\subset[0,1)\cap\mathbf{Q}. The natural morphism

H1​(𝔸θ1,FDel∙​DR⁡(N⊗Eθ))⟶HdR1​(𝔸θ1,N⊗Eθ)\mathrm{H}^{1}\bigl(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},F_{\mathrm{Del}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}\DR(N\otimes E^{\theta})\bigr)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},N\otimes E^{\theta})

is injective (see loc. cit.). Its image is denoted by Firr∙​HdR1​(𝔸θ1,N⊗Eθ)F_{\mathrm{irr}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},N\otimes E^{\theta}). The filtration Firr∙​HdR1​(𝔸θ1,N⊗Eθ)F_{\mathrm{irr}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},N\otimes E^{\theta}) behaves like in Definition 2.7 by additive convolution (see [27, Th. 3.39]).

Proposition 4.2 ([7, Prop. A.10]).

The functor NH↦(HdR1​(𝔸θ1,N⊗Eθ),Firr∙,W∙)N^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\bigl(\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta},N\otimes E^{\theta}),F_{\mathrm{irr}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}},W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}) from 𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸θ1)\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta}) to bifiltered vector spaces factors through Πθ\Pi_{\theta} and any morphism in 𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸θ1)\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\theta}) (or in 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS) yields a strictly bifiltered morphism.∎

5. Finite monodromic exponential mixed Hodge structures

This section continues Section 4 in the case where UU takes the form 𝔸s1×V\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{s}\times V and f=sm​gf=s^{m}g for some m⩾1m\geqslant 1 and some regular function g:V→𝔸1g:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1}. We first define the category 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲μ^\EMHS^{\widehat{\mu}} of finite monodromic exponential mixed Hodge structure. Then, in this particular case, H?∙​(U,f)\mathrm{H}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}_{?}(U,f) (?=c,∅,mid?={\mathrm{c}},\varnothing,{\mathrm{mid}}) is an object of 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲μ^\EMHS^{\widehat{\mu}}. We make explicit in geometric terms its classical and non-classical components (Proposition 5.10). The case where gg is moreover assumed to be tame is considered in Section 5.e, where the main objective is to provide tools for computing the irregular Hodge filtration on the corresponding de Rham cohomologies: for the classical component, Corollary 5.22 enables us to directly use results of [7, App.], while for the non-classical component, the main tool is provided by Corollary 5.32.

5.a. Constant exponential mixed Hodge structures

Let 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲cst\EMHS^{\mathrm{cst}} be the full subcategory of 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS consisting of objects whose associated 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-perverse sheaf belongs to 𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗏0cst\Perv_{0}^{\mathrm{cst}}. Since constant mixed Hodge modules on 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} are exactly those mixed Hodge modules whose associated perverse sheaf is constant (see [37, Th. 4.20]), we can as well define 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲cst\EMHS^{\mathrm{cst}} as the full subcategory of 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS consisting of objects whose restriction to 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} is a constant mixed Hodge module.

Lemma 5.1.

The functors

Hϕθ,1:𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲cst⟼𝖬𝖧𝖲andΠ∘Hi!:𝖬𝖧𝖲⟼𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲cst{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\phi_{\theta,1}:\EMHS^{\mathrm{cst}}\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\MHS\quad\text{and}\quad\Pi\circ{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}i_{!}:\MHS\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\EMHS^{\mathrm{cst}}

are mutually quasi-inverse equivalences of tensor categories strictly compatible with weight filtrations.

Proof.

It follows from Lemma 3.5 that 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲cst\EMHS^{\mathrm{cst}} is the essential image of Π∘Hi!\Pi\circ\,{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}i_{!}. The remaining statements were already observed in [7, Lem. A.12]. ∎

On 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲μ^\EMHS^{\widehat{\mu}}, the functor ψθ,≠1H{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\psi_{\theta,\neq 1} takes values in 𝖬𝖧𝖲⁡(μ^)\MHS({\widehat{\mu}}) by its very definition (see [31]), where the notation 𝖬𝖧𝖲⁡(μ^)\MHS({\widehat{\mu}}) is explained in Section 2. Proposition 5.2.

The functor

ϕμ^θH=(ϕθ,1H⊕ψμ^θ,≠1H):𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲μ^⟼𝖬𝖧𝖲μ^{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\phi_{\theta}^{\widehat{\mu}}=({}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\phi_{\theta,1}\oplus{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\psi_{\theta,\neq 1}^{\widehat{\mu}}):\EMHS^{\widehat{\mu}}\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\MHS^{\widehat{\mu}}

Definition 5.3 (Classical component).

For an object NHN^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} of 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲μ^\EMHS^{\widehat{\mu}}, its classical component NclH∈𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲cstN^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}_{\mathrm{cl}}\in\EMHS^{\mathrm{cst}} corresponds to the mixed Hodge structure ϕθ,1H​NH{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\phi_{\theta,1}N^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}. Proof of Proposition 5.2.

We mimic the definition in the proof of Lemma 3.6 to construct a quasi-inverse functor. Let (VH,G)(V^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}},G) be an object of 𝖬𝖧𝖲⁡(μ^)\MHS({\widehat{\mu}}), with G=𝐙/m​𝐙G=\mathbf{Z}/m\mathbf{Z}. We associate with it the object

([m]∗H(Π(i!HVH)))inv,\bigl({}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}[m]_{*}(\Pi({}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}i_{!}V^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}))\bigr)^{\mathrm{inv}},

where inv{\mathrm{inv}} means the invariant submodule with respect to the action of G−1×G′G^{-1}\times G^{\prime}. The proof of the equivalence property is then similar to that of loc. cit. That ϕμ^θH{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\phi_{\theta}^{\widehat{\mu}} is compatible with the tensor product of each category is similar to [34, Th. (8.11)],22 2 We can apply loc. cit. since the monodromy is finite, hence semi-simple, see [4, Rem. 6.6(ii)]. and can also be deduced from the more general result [18, Th. 1.2]. ∎

For an object NHN^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} of 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲≠1μ^\EMHS^{\widehat{\mu}}_{\neq 1} (i.e., having a classical component equal to zero), we have W∙EMHS​NH=W∙​NHW_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{EMHS}}N^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}=W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}N^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} since the underlying 𝐂[θ]⟨∂θ⟩\mathbf{C}[\theta]\langle\partial_{\theta}\rangle-module NN does not have any constant sub-quotient. In particular, if N′H,N′′HN^{\prime{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}},N^{\prime\prime{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}} are pure of respective weights w′,w′′w^{\prime},w^{\prime\prime}, then their convolution product is pure of weight w′+w′′w^{\prime}+w^{\prime\prime}.

Proposition 5.5.

The negative Fourier transformation is induced by the isomorphism 𝐂[x]⟨∂x⟩→𝐂[z]⟨∂z⟩\mathbf{C}[x]\langle\partial_{x}\rangle\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbf{C}[z]\langle\partial_{z}\rangle defined by x↦∂zx\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}\partial_{z}, ∂x↦−z\partial_{x}\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}-z. That it can be obtained by ( ∗ ‣ 6.2) is proved in [17, App. 2, §1]. ∎

The 𝐂[z]⟨∂z⟩\mathbf{C}[z]\langle\partial_{z}\rangle-module Ain\mathrm{Ai}_{n} is a free 𝐂⁡[z]\mathbf{C}[z]-module of rank nn, with a connection ∇\nabla having singularity at ∞\infty only. Being the Fourier transform of a 𝐂[x]⟨∂x⟩\mathbf{C}[x]\langle\partial_{x}\rangle-module of rank one, thus irreducible, Ain\mathrm{Ai}_{n} is also irreducible. Furthermore, the sheaf of horizontal sections Ain∇\mathrm{Ai}_{n}^{\nabla} is the constant sheaf of rank nn on 𝔸z1​a​n\mathbb{A}^{\!1\mathrm{an}}_{z}. The differential Galois group of Ain\mathrm{Ai}_{n} is (see [13, Th. 4.2.7])

{SLn​(𝐂)if n is odd,Spn​(𝐂)if n is even.\begin{cases}\mathrm{SL}_{n}(\mathbf{C})&\text{if $n$ is odd},\\ \mathrm{Sp}_{n}(\mathbf{C})&\text{if $n$ is even}.\end{cases}

It follows that, for nn even, Ain\mathrm{Ai}_{n} is isomorphic to its dual module. More precisely, we have the following behaviour with respect to duality. We denote by Ain∨\mathrm{Ai}_{n}^{\scriptscriptstyle\vee} the dual 𝐂[z]⟨∂z⟩\mathbf{C}[z]\langle\partial_{z}\rangle-module. It is isomorphic to 𝐂[z]⟨∂z⟩/((−∂z)n−z)\mathbf{C}[z]\langle\partial_{z}\rangle/((-\partial_{z})^{n}-z).

7. Proof of Theorem 1.1

We consider from now on the classical Airy equation ∂z2−z\partial_{z}^{2}-z (the case n=2n=2 in Section 6), and we set Ai=Ai2\mathrm{Ai}=\mathrm{Ai}_{2} and f⁡(x,z)=13​x3−z​xf(x,z)=\frac{1}{3}x^{3}-zx. The strategy of the proof of Theorem 1.1 is very similar to that developed in [7] for the Kloosterman case. It consists of

  1. (1)

    exhibiting a natural basis of HdR1​(𝔸1,Symk⁡Ai)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathbb{A}^{\!1},\Sym^{k}\mathrm{Ai}) (Proposition 7.5 and Corollary 7.7);

  2. (2)

    showing that this basis is adapted to the irregular Hodge filtration by lifting it to a suitable compactification of 𝔸k+1\mathbb{A}^{\!k+1} and by computing order of poles of representative differential forms along components of the divisor at infinity;

  3. (3)

    showing that this basis induces a basis of each graded piece of the irregular Hodge filtration by means of a duality argument.

7.g. Proof of Proposition 7.20

Recall the map ρε\rho_{\varepsilon} defined by (7.19).

Proposition 7.29.

The Hodge bundles F∙​(M~k,ε)F^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}(\widetilde{M}_{k,\varepsilon}) satisfy, for ε∈𝐙/3​𝐙\varepsilon\in\mathbf{Z}/3\mathbf{Z},

rk⁡grFp​M~k,ε=#​ρε−1​(p)∀p.\rk\gr^{p}_{F}\widetilde{M}_{k,\varepsilon}=\#\rho_{\varepsilon}^{-1}(p)\quad\forall p.
Proof.

Since the monodromy of M~k\widetilde{M}_{k} at infinity is semi-simple, the limit mixed Hodge structure of M~kH\widetilde{M}_{k}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} at infinity is pure, and the graded pieces of the limit Hodge filtration have the same dimension as the corresponding graded pieces at a generic point of 𝔸τ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau}. In order to compute rk⁡grFp​M~k\rk\gr_{F}^{p}\widetilde{M}_{k}, we are thus led to computing the ranks for this limit Hodge filtration.

For that purpose, we use the comparison with the limit at t=0t=0 of the irregular Hodge filtration of Symk⁡Gg\Sym^{k}G_{g}, as proved in [28]33 3 We used this argument in the opposite direction in [29, (7)]. in order to take advantage of the property that the irregular Hodge filtration on Symk⁡Gg\Sym^{k}G_{g} is easily computed by means of the Thom-Sebastiani formula from that of GgG_{g}, hence is more directly accessible than the Hodge filtration of M~k\widetilde{M}_{k}.

We first compute the jumps of the irregular Hodge filtration Firr∙​Gg,1F^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}_{\mathrm{irr}}G_{g,1} of GgG_{g} at t=1t=1. Since g∗H​p​𝐐𝔸1H{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}g_{*}\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\mathbf{Q}}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}} is a pure Hodge module of weight 11, it corresponds, away from the singularities, to a polarizable variation of pure Hodge structure of weight zero on 𝔸τ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau}. The eigenvalues of the monodromy at τ=∞\tau=\infty of the non constant part of g+​O𝔸1g_{+}{O}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}} (the constant part has rank one and is given by the trace) being exp(±2π𝗂/3)\exp(\pm 2\pi\mathsf{i}/3), the irregular Hodge filtration Firr∙​Gg,1F^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}_{\mathrm{irr}}G_{g,1} jumps at 1/31/3 and 2/32/3 (see [29, (7)]).

In order to compute the jumps of the irregular Hodge filtration of j+​Kζ,t⊗Symk⁡Ggj^{+}K_{\zeta,t}\otimes\Sym^{k}G_{g}, we use that this filtration is obtained by tensor product from the irregular Hodge filtration of Kζ,tK_{\zeta,t} and that of Symk⁡Gg\Sym^{k}G_{g} (Thom-Sebastiani).

On the one hand, by the same Thom-Sebastiani argument and the computation above, the jumps of Firr∙​Symk​Gg,1F_{\mathrm{irr}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}\Sym^{k}G_{g,1} occur exactly at λ=(i+2​j)/3\lambda=(i+2j)/3 where i,ji,j vary from 00 to kk and i+j=ki+j=k. We write λ=k/3+j/3\lambda=k/3+j/3 with jj varying from 00 to kk.

On the other hand, if ε≠0\varepsilon\neq 0, we regard Kζ−1,τK_{\zeta^{-1},\tau} on 𝔸τ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau} as a complex Hodge module of rank one with Hodge filtration jumping at p=0p=0 only. Then, by [29, (7)], the irregular Hodge filtration of its localized Fourier transform Kζ,tK_{\zeta,t} on 𝔾m,t\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},t} jumps at α\alpha only, with α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) and α≡ε/3mod1\alpha\equiv\varepsilon/3\bmod 1. By using once more the good behaviour of FirrF_{\mathrm{irr}} under tensor product, we find similarly that the jumps of Firr∙​(j+​Kζ,t⊗Symk⁡Gg)F_{\mathrm{irr}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}(j^{+}K_{\zeta,t}\otimes\Sym^{k}G_{g}) occur exactly at λ=k/3+j/3+ε/3\lambda=k/3+j/3+\varepsilon/3, where jj varies from 00 to kk and ε/3∈(0,1)\varepsilon/3\in(0,1).

Since rk⁡Symk⁡Gg=k+1\rk\Sym^{k}G_{g}=k+1, this implies that the jumps are all equal to one. For applying the inverse stationary phase formula, we do not care of the jumps at integers, and the one-dimensional jumps of Firr∙​(j+​Kζ,t⊗Symk⁡Gg)F_{\mathrm{irr}}^{\raisebox{1.0pt}{${\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}$}}(j^{+}K_{\zeta,t}\otimes\Sym^{k}G_{g}) (ε∈𝐙/3​𝐙\varepsilon\in\mathbf{Z}/3\mathbf{Z}) at p+1/3p+1/3, resp. p+2/3p+2/3 for p∈𝐙p\in\mathbf{Z} occur respectively for

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
